key_concept: The bones of the human lower limb run proximal to distal as femur (thigh), patella (kneecap, in front of the knee joint), tibia and fibula (leg), tarsals (ankle), metatarsals and phalanges.
steps: Each lower limb has 30 bones: femur (1), tibia and fibula (2), patella (1), tarsals (7), metatarsals (5) and phalanges (14).
Start at the hip. The femur is the thigh bone, the longest bone of the body, and it articulates with the acetabulum of the pelvic girdle.

At the knee, the patella (kneecap) is a sesamoid bone lying in front of the joint between the lower end of the femur and the upper end of the tibia. So in a proximal-to-distal sequence it comes between the femur and the tibia.
Below the knee is the leg, made of the tibia and fibula. The tibia is the main weight-bearing bone.
The tibia then articulates with the tarsals (ankle bones; the talus forms the ankle joint).
So the sequence is Femur → Patella → Tibia → Tarsal, which is option (3). This matches the official key.
why_not_others: Option (1) places the patella after the tibia, but the patella sits at the knee, between the femur and tibia. Option (2) puts the patella above the femur, and option (4) puts the tarsals before the knee bones, so neither follows the proximal-to-distal order.
common_trap: Students often forget the patella, or place it below the tibia, because it is not part of the long-bone chain and sits in front of the knee joint.
time_saving_tip: The sequence must start at the hip with the femur, which eliminates option (2). Then ask where the kneecap is: between the thigh and the leg. That gives option (3) directly.
